record.paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
record.original_question: If F is a free group and H ✁ F with F/H right-orderable, then is F/[H, H] orderable?

evidence.quote: 3.6. If F is a free group and H ✁ F with F/H right orderable, then is F/[H, H] orderable?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a free group and let $H$ be a normal subgroup of $F$. Recall that a group $G$ is right-orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication, i.e., $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a,b,c \in G$; and $G$ is orderable (bi-orderable) if there exists a total order on $G$ invariant under both left and right multiplication. Let $[H,H]$ denote the commutator subgroup of $H$ (which is normal in $F$ since $H$ is normal in $F$).

Suppose the quotient $F/H$ is right-orderable. Determine whether the quotient $F/[H,H]$ is necessarily orderable (bi-orderable).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem appears in a known collection of unsolved problems on ordered and orderable groups. Web searches did not surface a published resolution; related results (e.g., on soluble right-orderable groups being locally indicable, and the bi-orderability of free groups and certain commutator quotients) are available, but no source confirms a complete answer to the specific question of whether $F/[H,H]$ is orderable whenever $F/H$ is right-orderable. Status is therefore unverified.

status_evidence.title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
status_evidence.snippet: Lists the question as an unsolved problem about quotients of free groups by commutator subgroups of normal subgroups with right-orderable quotient.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is listed among open problems on orderable groups.

status_evidence.title: Soluble right orderable groups are locally indicable
status_evidence.snippet: Establishes that soluble right-orderable groups are locally indicable, a result relevant to orderability of metabelian-like quotients.
status_evidence.claim: Related orderability theorems exist but do not directly resolve the question.
